On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under:
1. Whether the injured master Roshan Kumar Sharma suffered injures in a road traffic accident on 13.03.2018 due to rash an

Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence ar

Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287

Reliance is placed on the observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravi vs. Badrinarayan & ors., (Civil appeal no. 196/2011, arising out of SLP (C) No. 11974 of 2008,
decided on 18.02.2011):
"20.
It is well settled that delay in lodging FIR cannot be a ground to doubt the claimants case.
Knowing the Indian conditions as they are, we cannot expect a common man to first rush to the police station immediately after an accident.
Human nature and family responsibilities occupy the mind of kith and kin to such an extent that they give more importance to get the victim treated rather to rush to the police station.
Under such circumstances, they are not expected to act mechanically with promptitude in lodging the FIR with the police.
Delay in lodging the FIR thus, cannot be the ground to deny justice to victim.
In cases of delay, the Courts are required to examine the evidence with a closer scrutiny and doing so, the contents of the FIR should be scrutinized more carefully.

If Court finds that there is no indication of fabrication or it has not been concocted or engineered to implicate innocent person,
then, even if there is a delay in lodging the FIR, the claim case cannot be dismissed merely on that ground."
During cross examination on this aspect, PW1 replied that he was taken to such hospital by the driver of the offending vehicle.
This response of PW1 has not been refuted by any counter suggestion.

The proof of the document has been disputed by the respondents only because such document is a photocopy and accordingly marked as Mark-A. Such document even if not read in evidence would not defeat the claim as an averment as to an acciden

Further, Mark A is a document prepared in the regular course at a government hospital, which also forms a part of the charge sheet and DAR Ex.PW1/1.
15.
The DAR, Ex.PW1/1 refers to a document/letter addressed by the IO to the CMO, Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital seeking opinion as to the injury.
This document also contains a verification from the concerned hospital by the IO regarding treatment of patient Raushan Kumar in emergency on 13.03.2018 at 01:31 PM.
In view of such verification by the IO, there is no reason to doubt the emergency treatment card merely because it is a photocopy document.
16. Further such document shows that the injured was taken to hospital on the same date of the accident within 1  hour of the accident.
The history of injury as disclosed to the the doctor is also noted as RTA (Road Traffic Accident).
Another document i.e. OPD ticket dated 19.03.2018, filed with the DAR after the injured was referred to Ortho OPD, notes the injury as "laceration over dorsum of foot with fracture in MT(R)".

Thus, even though no x-ray report of fracture has been filed,
the document annexed with the DAR is sufficient to prove fracture sustained by the injured Raushan Kumar.
Thus, injury so sustained by the claimant is grievous in nature.

17. In the present case, police after investigation had filed charge sheet against Respondent no. 1 under Section 279/338 of IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent in causing the accident.
The IO has filed Detailed Accident Report before this Tribunal.

In National Insurance Co.
vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle.

18. It may further be noted that in Cholamandalam Insurance Company vs. Kamlesh, 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310, it was held that if the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him.
In the present case also, driver did not enter into the witness box to controvert the claim of petitioner or even to explain circumstances of accident.
19. On perusal of the evidence led by the petitioner, it is seen that PW1 has deposed on the lines of police investigation and nothing material has come on record to refute his claim.

Thus, having regard to the parameters of standard of proof in the case of present nature, filing of charge sheet against Respondent no.1, Respondent no.1 not stepping into the witness box and the evidence proved on record
, it is held that the accident in question is caused due to the rash and negligent driving of Respondent no.1.
Accordingly, Issue no. 1 is decided in favour of the petitioner.
Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?

At this stage, before proceeding further, by rely upon the judgments of C.K. Subramania Iyer v.
T. Kunhikuttan Nair, R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. and Baker v. Willoughby which are referred and relied in Raj Kumar Vs. Aja
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life,
his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could hav

21. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
n
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

21.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv).

21.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of futu
21.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence.

21.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof.
21.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves d
Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary.

21.6. It was observed by Hon'ble Sc in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii) (a).
21.7.
We are not concerned with assessment regarding loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability in this case, as petitioner did not suffer any permanent disability.
22. PW-1/ father of minor injured child deposed that his son i.e. injured was 12 years of age at the time of accident.
He has relied upon Aadhar Card of the injured as Ex.PW1/4 to show date of birth of the injured as 11.11.2004.
Since the accident occurred on 13.03.2018, the injured would have been around 13  years of age.
The injured is nowhere claimed to be studying or that he was incapacitated from attending any school.
It is further deposed that the injured sustained a fracture in his right leg as well as injuries for which he was treated at Pandit Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital and continues to take treatment.
During cross examination, however, PW1 admitted that his son was not receiving any medical treatment and is medically fit.
MLC mark A as well as OPD ticket (annexure to Ex.PW1/1 (DAR)) proves pain and swelling in the right foot, laceration over dorsum of foot and observes fracture (# 2nd MT(R)).
At the same time, no proof of continuous treatment or permanent disability has been filed to conclude so.
